@graph.headline: What Are the Strangest Animals in the Galápagos?

mainEntity.name: What is the strangest animal in the Galápagos?

acceptedAnswer.text: There's no single answer, but the marine iguana is a strong contender: it's the only lizard on Earth that feeds in the sea, grazing algae off underwater rocks and sneezing out the salt it swallows. That diving, salt-sneezing lifestyle exists nowhere else.

mainEntity.name: Why are Galápagos animals so unusual and found nowhere else?

acceptedAnswer.text: The islands sit about 600 miles offshore, isolated by deep ocean and ranging in age from older east to youngest west. Species arrived rarely, then evolved in place — often on a single island. The result: about 80% of land birds and 97% of reptiles are endemic.

mainEntity.name: Are there really penguins in the Galápagos?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The Galápagos penguin is the only penguin that lives at the equator, with part of its range in the northern hemisphere. About 95% live around Fernandina and western Isabela, with smaller numbers on Bartolomé, Floreana and Santiago. Cold currents make their tropical home possible.

mainEntity.name: Is there a finch that drinks blood?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — the vampire finch on remote Wolf Island pecks at the base of nesting seabirds' feathers and drinks their blood, likely an evolution from eating parasites off the birds. Wolf is a far-northern island reachable only by liveaboard dive trips, so few travellers ever encounter it.

mainEntity.name: What is the pink iguana and where does it live?

acceptedAnswer.text: The pink land iguana is a Critically Endangered species of only about 350 animals, living solely on Wolf Volcano at the northern tip of Isabela. Its range is permit-restricted and effectively closed to visitors — part of why it was only described in recent decades.

mainEntity.name: Why do marine iguanas sneeze or spit salt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because they feed in the sea, marine iguanas swallow a lot of salt. A special nasal gland concentrates it, and they "sneeze" it out in a fine spray — which often lands back on their heads, leaving the white crusts you'll see on basking animals.

mainEntity.name: Is a Galápagos fur seal a seal or a sea lion?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a sea lion, despite the name. The Galápagos fur seal is the smaller and shier of the archipelago's two eared seals, and it prefers cool, shaded, rocky shores. Look for it in the western islands, at James Bay on Santiago and Darwin Bay on Genovesa.

mainEntity.name: Which Galápagos animals are found only there?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many. Overall the archipelago has more than 1,300 endemic species. Standouts include the marine iguana, flightless cormorant, Galápagos penguin, pink land iguana and vampire finch — the last two on a single volcano and island respectively. About 97% of reptiles and land mammals are endemic.

mainEntity.name: Are Galápagos animals dangerous or afraid of people?

acceptedAnswer.text: They're famously unafraid, because they evolved with few predators — but that's not an invitation to approach. Park rules require staying at least 2 metres from wildlife and touring protected sites with a certified naturalist guide. Keep your distance and let them ignore you.

mainEntity.name: Can you see these species on any trip?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on where and when you go. Many are tied to specific islands or seasons — waved albatross are on Española only about April to December, and Wolf's species need a dive liveaboard. Wildlife calendars are approximate, and no sighting is ever guaranteed.
